    Let ρ\rho be a (not necessarily invariant) density operator with tr⁡(ρ​I​F^)=f{\rm tr}(\rho\widehat{I\hskip-3.9ptF})=f, 1<f<d1<f<d and co⁡(ε⁡(f))=ε⁡(f){\rm co}(\varepsilon(f))=\varepsilon(f). Then with suitably chosen α,β∈I​R\alpha,\beta\in{{\rm I\mkern-3.6muR}}

    ρ~=(α​1​I+β​I​F^)∗​ρ​(α​1​I+β​I​F^)\widetilde{\rho}=(\alpha{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}+\beta\widehat{I\hskip-3.9ptF})^{*}\rho(\alpha{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}+\beta\widehat{I\hskip-3.9ptF}) (60)

    is a density operator with tr⁡(ρ~​I​F^)=1{\rm tr}(\widetilde{\rho}\widehat{I\hskip-3.9ptF})=1. Suppose that ρ~\widetilde{\rho} is separable. Then formula (59) also holds for ρ\rho.

  • •

    If ff satisfies co⁡(ε⁡(f))<ε⁡(f){\rm co}(\varepsilon(f))<\varepsilon(f) , the convex hull has a flat section between f1<f<f2f_{1}<f<f_{2} where f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} are the two end points of the flat piece satisfying co⁡(ε⁡(f1/2))=ε⁡(f1/2){\rm co}(\varepsilon(f_{1/2}))=\varepsilon(f_{1/2}). We can always find a convex decomposition of ρ\rho in two states with expectation values f1,f2f_{1},f_{2}. If now the above procedure works for these two states, then we have found an optimal decomposition for ρ\rho and can easily compute the entanglement of formation.

IV.5 Results for O​OOO-invariant states

Here the extension method of Section IV.B turns out to do much of the work. The state space, plotted in Figure 7, is separated in four regions. The separable square and the three triangles A,B,CA,B,C.

In order to apply the extension method to the U​UUU-invariant states, we have to see which states can be written as ρ=(x​1​I+y​I​F)​ρ~​(x​1​I+y​I​F)∗\rho=(x{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}+y{I\hskip-3.9ptF}){\widetilde{\rho}}(x{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}+y{I\hskip-3.9ptF})^{*}, with ρ~{\widetilde{\rho}} a separable state with flip expectation zero. If we take for ρ~{\widetilde{\rho}} any state at the left edge of the separable square, it is clear that we will get an O​OOO-invariant state again. The explicit computation shows that with this method we get EF​(ρ)E_{\rm F}(\rho) in the full triangle BB. Note that by this construction EF​(ρ)E_{\rm F}(\rho) depends only on the expectation ⟨I​F⟩\langle{I\hskip-3.9ptF}\rangle, and not on ⟨I​F^⟩\langle\widehat{I\hskip-3.9ptF}\rangle or the dimension dd. Employing similarly the extension method for U​U¯U\overline{U} we find EF​(ρ)E_{\rm F}(\rho) in the triangle AA, getting a function depending only on ⟨I​F^⟩\langle\widehat{I\hskip-3.9ptF}\rangle and the dimension, but not on ⟨I​F⟩\langle{I\hskip-3.9ptF}\rangle.

IV.6 Results for Bell-States

The Bell-States were one of the first classes for which entanglement of formation could be calculated [9]. Of course, our method reproduces this result, albeit with a more economical decomposition. This is a feature shared with the Wootters formula[10]. It is a natural question whether the extension method, applied in this basic example, reproduces the Wootters formula. However, it turns out that one gets the result only on state manifolds of lower dimension. We also did not succeed in finding another group of local symmetries, which would give Wootter’s formula in full generality.

V Relative Entropy of Entanglement

V.1 Simplified computation

Symmetry simplifies the computation of the relative entropy of entanglement dramatically: it reduces the variation in (33) from a variation over all separable states σ∈𝒟\sigma\in{\cal D} to those, which are also GG-invariant. i.e., when ρ=𝐏​ρ\rho={\bf P}\rho, we have

ERE​(ρ)=inf{   S​(ρ,σ)|σ∈𝐏​𝒟}.E_{\rm RE}(\rho)=\inf\big\{{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\sigma)\big|\sigma\in{\bf P}{\cal D}\big\}\;. (61)

The only ingredients of the proof are the convexity of σ↦   S​(ρ,σ)\sigma\mapsto{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\sigma), the invariance of relative entropy under (local) unitary transformations of both its arguments, and that 𝒟{\cal D} is a convex set invariant under local unitaries. Indeed, the properties of 𝒟{\cal D} imply that for any σ\sigma in the full variational problem, 𝐏​σ∈𝐏​𝒟⊂𝒟{\bf P}\sigma\in{\bf P}{\cal D}\subset{\cal D} is also a legitimate argument, and the convexity properties of    S show that this cannot increase    S​(ρ,σ){\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\sigma). Hence the variation may be restricted as in (61). We have listed the ingredients of the proof so explicitly, because many variations of EREE_{\rm RE} may be of interest. For example, the “distance” function relative entropy can be replaced by a host of other functions, like norm differences of any kind. The set 𝒟{\cal D}, too, may be replaced, for example by the set of ppt-states, as suggested by Rains [13], who also made similar use of symmetry.

A second simplification concerns the computation of    S​(ρ,σ){\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\sigma) itself, when both arguments are GG-invariant. We have seen that GG-invariant states can be considered as states on the commutant algebra G′G^{\prime}. Now the relative entropy is defined for pairs of states on arbitrary C*-algebras [19], and the form (32) involving density matrices is only the special form valid for a full matrix algebra. Since 𝐏{\bf P} is a conditional expectation onto G′G^{\prime}, the result does not depend [19] on whether we compute the relative entropy via density matrices, or for the corresponding abstract linear functionals on G′G^{\prime}. Without going into the details for general algebras G′G^{\prime} here, let us see how this helps in the case when G′G^{\prime} is abelian, as in most of our examples.

Suppose pαp_{\alpha}, α=1,…,N\alpha=1,\ldots,N are the minimal projections of G′G^{\prime}, and denote by ωα=(tr​pα)−1​pα\omega_{\alpha}=({\rm tr}p_{\alpha})^{-1}p_{\alpha} the extremal density matrices of 𝐏​𝒮{\bf P}{\cal S}. Then every ρ∈𝐏​𝒮\rho\in{\bf P}{\cal S} has a unique representation as a convex combination

ρ=∑αρα​ωα=∑αραtr​pα​pα,\rho=\sum_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha}\omega_{\alpha}=\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\rho_{\alpha}}{{\rm tr}p_{\alpha}}\ p_{\alpha}\;, (62)

where the second expression is at the same time the spectral resolution of ρ\rho. If we compute the von Neumann entropy −tr⁡(ρ​log⁡ρ)-{\rm tr}(\rho\log\rho) from this, we find a dependence of the result not only on the expectations ρα=tr⁡(ρ​pα)\rho_{\alpha}={\rm tr}(\rho p_{\alpha}), but also on the multiplicities tr⁡(pα){\rm tr}(p_{\alpha}), as is quite familiar from statistical mechanics. On the other hand, the fact that relative entropy can be defined for states on abstract algebras shows that no such dependence can occur for relative entropies. Indeed, the terms involving log⁡tr⁡(pα)\log{\rm tr}(p_{\alpha}) from ρ\rho and σ\sigma cancel, and we get

   S​(ρ,σ)=∑αρα​(log⁡(ρα)−log⁡(σα)),{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\sigma)=\sum_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha}\Bigl(\log(\rho_{\alpha})-\log(\sigma_{\alpha})\Bigr)\;, (63)

where ρα\rho_{\alpha} and σα\sigma_{\alpha} are the respective expectations of pαp_{\alpha}.

A typical application is the observation that for U​UUU-invariant states the expression for the relative entropy of entanglement can be written down in terms of the tr⁡(ρ​F){\rm tr}(\rho F), independently of the dimension dd of the underlying Hilbert spaces.

For U​UUU and U​U¯U\overline{U}-invariant states the sets of separable states are just intervals, and the definition of relative entropy of entanglement requires a minimization over this interval. However, due to a general property of the relative entropy, the convexity in both arguments, it is clear that the minimum is, in fact always obtained at the endpoint: if ρ\rho is the state whose entanglement we want to calculate, and σ\sigma is the minimizing separable state, convexity implies

 S​(ρ,λ​σ+(1−λ)​ρ)\displaystyle{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\lambda\sigma+(1-\lambda)\rho) ≤\displaystyle\leq λ​ S​(ρ,σ)+(1−λ)​ S​(ρ,ρ)\displaystyle\lambda{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\sigma)+(1-\lambda){\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\rho)
=\displaystyle= λ​ S​(ρ,σ).\displaystyle\lambda{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho,\sigma)\;.

Hence if there were any separable state on the straight line segment connecting ρ\rho and σ\sigma, it would give a strictly lower minimum, contradicting the minimality of σ\sigma.

For U​UUU the boundary separable state has tr⁡(σ​I​F)=0{\rm tr}(\sigma{I\hskip-3.9ptF})=0, i.e., gives equal weight to the minimal projections. We have to compute the relative entropy with respect to a state with probabilities (1±f)/2(1\pm f)/2, i.e., the function

eRE​(f)=log⁡2−S⁡(1+f2,1−f2),e_{\rm RE}(f)=\log 2-S\left(\frac{1+f}{2},\frac{1-f}{2}\right)\;, (64)

where we denote by S(p1,…,pn)=−∑kpklogpkS(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})=-\sum_{k}p_{k}\log p_{k} the entropy of a probability vector (p1,…,pn)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}). This function is plotted in Figure 8, and determines the relative entropy of entanglement of U​UUU-symmetric states ρ\rho via

ERE​(ρ)=eRE​(tr⁡(ρ​I​F)).E_{\rm RE}(\rho)=e_{\rm RE}\bigl({\rm tr}(\rho{I\hskip-3.9ptF})\bigr)\;. (65)

Similarly, the boundary point σ\sigma of 𝒟{\cal D} for U​U¯U\overline{U} invariant states is given by tr⁡(σ​I​F^)=1{\rm tr}(\sigma\widehat{I\hskip-3.9ptF})=1. For general f^=tr⁡(ρ​I​F^)\widehat{f}={\rm tr}(\rho\widehat{I\hskip-3.9ptF}) the minimal projections have weights f^/d\widehat{f}/d and (1−f^/d)(1-\widehat{f}/d). Hence for U​U¯U\overline{U}-symmetric ρ\rho, we have ERE​(ρ)=0E_{\rm RE}(\rho)=0 for f^≤1\widehat{f}\leq 1, and

log⁡d−(1−f^d)​log⁡(d−1)−S⁡(f^d,1−f^d)\log d-(1-\frac{\widehat{f}}{d})\log(d-1)-S\Bigl(\frac{\widehat{f}}{d},1-\frac{\widehat{f}}{d}\Bigr) (66)

otherwise. For comparison with the results of [12], note that f^/d\widehat{f}/d is the so called maximally entangled fraction of ρ\rho.

Now we look at O​OOO-invariant states. The state space and the separable states are drawn in Figure 7. First we look at the state with the coordinates (1,3)(1,3), which is a maximal entangled state. The separable states, that are minimizing the relative entropy for this state, are the states on the whole line connecting the points (0,1)(0,1) and (1,1)(1,1). But now we can find the minimizing separable for any state in the whole triangle AA. We just have to draw the straight line connecting the coordinates of a given states with the point (1,3)(1,3). The intersection with the border of 𝐏​𝒟{\bf P}{\cal D} is then a minimizer for (1,3)(1,3) and by the properties of the relative entropy of entanglement also the minimizer for all states on the connecting line. The same argumentation works for the edge point (−1,0)(-1,0) and the separable border between (0,0)(0,0) and (0,1)(0,1) giving us all minimizers for the triangle BB. The whole triangle CC has the same minimizer, namely (0,1)(0,1).

V.2 Counterexample to additivity

To find a counterexample to the additivity of the relative entropy of entanglement we use the group introduced in Example 7 . We also know that additivity will hold for any states where one of the two independently prepared states is separable. So in our example we can restrict to the area, where both expectation values of F1F_{1} and F2F_{2} are negative.

For simplicity we increase the group with I​FAlice⊗I​FBob{I\hskip-3.9ptF}_{\rm Alice}\otimes{I\hskip-3.9ptF}_{\rm Bob} leading us to a smaller commutant only spanned by 1​I⊗1​I,I​F⊗I​F,1​I⊗I​F+I​F⊗1​I{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}\otimes{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}},{I\hskip-3.9ptF}\otimes{I\hskip-3.9ptF},{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}\otimes{I\hskip-3.9ptF}+{I\hskip-3.9ptF}\otimes{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}. As coordinate system we use the expectation values of

F\displaystyle F =\displaystyle= 12​(1​I⊗I​F+I​F⊗1​I)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}({{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}\otimes{I\hskip-3.9ptF}+{I\hskip-3.9ptF}\otimes{{\rm 1\mkern-5.4muI}}) (67)
F12\displaystyle F_{12} =\displaystyle= I​F⊗I​F.\displaystyle{I\hskip-3.9ptF}\otimes{I\hskip-3.9ptF}. (68)

The state space is drawn in Figure 9.

It is just the intersection of the state space of the original group (see Figure 4) with the plane given by ⟨F1⟩=⟨F2⟩=⟨F⟩\langle F_{1}\rangle=\langle F_{2}\rangle=\langle F\rangle. The product states, in the sense of additivity, are given by the line (⟨F⟩,⟨F⟩2)(\langle F\rangle,\langle F\rangle^{2}).

The counterexample we want to look at, is the state referring to the coordinates (−1,1)(-1,1), which is given by ρ−⊗ρ−\rho_{-}\otimes\rho_{-} where ρ−\rho_{-} denotes the normalized projection on the antisymmetric subspace of   Cd⊗  Cd{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.45831pt,depth=-0.43057pt,width=0.2pt\kern-3.00003pt\rm C}}^{d}\otimes{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.45831pt,depth=-0.43057pt,width=0.2pt\kern-3.00003pt\rm C}}^{d}. From Equation (65) we know the relative entropy of entanglement for ρ−\rho_{-} to be log⁡2\log 2 independent from the dimension dd. The minimizing state was the state with flip expectation value equal to zero now denoted as ρ0\rho_{0}. So the expected minimizer for the tensor product would be ρ0⊗ρ0\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{0} located on the quadratic product line with the expectation values (0,0)(0,0). This one gives us the expected value of log⁡4\log 4 for the relative entropy. Now we calculate the relative entropy between ρ−⊗2=ρ−⊗ρ−\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2}=\rho_{-}\otimes\rho_{-} and ρ#\rho_{\#}.

 S​(ρ−⊗2,ρ#)\displaystyle{\hbox{\kern 3.00003pt\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=-3.44444pt,width=0.5pt\kern 0.89996pt\vrule height=3.01385pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.5pt\kern-3.30002pt\rm S}}(\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2},\rho_{\#}) =\displaystyle= tr⁡(ρ−⊗2​log⁡ρ−⊗2−ρ−⊗2​log⁡ρ#)\displaystyle{\rm tr}(\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2}\log\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2}-\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2}\log\rho_{\#}) (69)
=\displaystyle= tr⁡(ρ−⊗2​log⁡ρ−⊗2−ρ−⊗2​log⁡d−12​d​ρ−⊗2)\displaystyle{\rm tr}(\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2}\log\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2}-\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2}\log\frac{d-1}{2d}\rho_{-}^{\otimes 2}) (70)
=\displaystyle= −log⁡d−12​d=log⁡4−log⁡2​(d−1)d.\displaystyle-\log\frac{d-1}{2d}=\log 4-\log\frac{2(d-1)}{d}\;. (71)

Indeed the minimum must be attained on the line connecting ρ0⊗ρ0\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{0} and ρ#\rho_{\#} and it can easily be verified, that the minimum always is attained on ρ#\rho_{\#}. For d=2d=2 the whole line gives the same value and although there exits minimizer not belonging to the product space, additivity holds. For d>2d>2 the expectation values of state ρ#\rho_{\#} given by (1d,1)(\frac{1}{d},1) shift near to the F12F_{12} axis and from a geometrical point of view closer to ρ−⊗ρ−\rho_{-}\otimes\rho_{-}. Although the relative entropy is not a real kind of geometrical measure this intuition did not fail. In these cases the additivity is violated with an amount of log⁡2​(d−1)d\log\frac{2(d-1)}{d}. For very high dimension dd we get the really surprising result ER​E​(ρ−⊗ρ−)≃ER​E​(ρ−)E_{RE}(\rho_{-}\otimes\rho_{-})\simeq E_{RE}(\rho_{-}).

VI Concluding Remarks

We have concentrated on just two basic entanglement measures. Clearly, there are many more, and for many of them the computation can be simplified for symmetric states. Among these measures of entanglement are the “best separable approximation” of a state [20], the trace norm of the partial transpose [21], the base norm associated with 𝒟{\cal D} (called cross norm in [22] and absolute robustness in [23]). For distillible entanglement we refer to the recent paper of Rains [6]. Similarly, there is a lot of work left to be done carrying out the programme outlined in this paper for all the groups of local symmetries listed in Section II.1.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
